title: Homestay Website SEO: Location Pages, Titles and Schema
excerpt: How to plan homestay website SEO: location and experience pages, title tags, LodgingBusiness schema, local tourism links and avoiding thin duplicate pages.
description: Homestay website SEO in plain terms: location and "how to reach" pages, title tags, LodgingBusiness schema, local links and avoiding thin pages.
html:
Homestay website SEO means building pages that match how travellers search: a page for each room type, location pages such as "things to do near" and "how to reach", clear title tags, LodgingBusiness schema, and links from local tourism sites. Each page must say something useful and different, not repeat the same text for every nearby town.

What travellers actually search for

Travellers rarely search for your homestay's name until someone has told them about it. They search for the place and the kind of stay: "homestay in Chikmagalur with estate view", "pet friendly stay near Coorg", "how to reach Dzongu from Gangtok", "things to do near Vythiri in monsoon". Your website should have a clear, useful page for each of those intentions that you genuinely serve.

A small homestay site does not need hundreds of pages. Ten to twenty well-written pages usually cover the main searches: the home page, each room type, food and experiences, location and travel, a few local guides, and contact. Your Google Business Profile handles map searches; see our guide to homestay Google Business Profile and Maps visibility for that side.

The pages a homestay website needs

PageSearch it servesWhat it must include
Home page"homestay in <place>", your namePlace name, type of stay, best photo, who it suits, how to book
Rooms (one page per type)"family room homestay <place>", "cottage with view"Beds, capacity, bathroom, view, photos, what is included
Food and experiences"homestay with home food <place>", "plantation walk"Meals served, dietary options, activities and timings
How to reach"how to reach <place> from Bengaluru"Routes from main cities, nearest station and airport, road conditions, taxi options
Things to do nearby"things to do near <place>"Sights with real distances and travel times, seasons, your own tips
Seasonal guide"<place> in monsoon", "best time to visit <place>"Weather by month, what is open, what to pack
Contact and bookingYour name plus "contact" or "booking"Phone, WhatsApp, address, map, policies

Location and experience pages that rank and help

Location pages are where a homestay can beat bigger sites, because you know the area better than any travel portal. Write them from local knowledge.

"How to reach" pages

Give routes from your main source cities, in the order guests ask: by car, by train, by bus, by air. Include the last stretch honestly: whether the road is narrow, whether small cars manage it in monsoon, where mobile signal drops, and where to call you from. Add the nearest fuel station and ATM. This is the kind of detail travellers bookmark and share.

"Things to do near" pages

List places you would actually send a guest, with realistic travel time from your gate, the best time of day to go, entry details if you know them well, and a line on who will enjoy it. Add your own photos where you can. A page about the waterfalls, treks and coffee tours near your Sakleshpur homestay, written from experience, is far more useful than a generic list copied from a travel site.

Experience pages

If you offer something specific, such as a Kodava meal, a birdwatching walk, a tea factory visit or a village homestay programme in Nagaland, give it its own page with what happens, how long it takes, the season and the cost or whether it is included.

Title tags and meta descriptions, simply

The title tag is the blue headline Google shows in results. The meta description is the short text below it, though Google sometimes writes its own. For each page:

  • Put the main idea first: "Coffee Estate Homestay in Chikmagalur with Valley View".
  • Keep titles short enough to show in full, roughly under 60 characters.
  • Make every page's title different. Ten pages titled "Home | Green Valley Homestay" tell Google nothing.
  • Write the meta description as a reason to click: what the page answers or offers, in one or two sentences.
  • Use one clear heading at the top of each page that matches the title.

Schema markup explained simply

Schema is a small block of code, invisible to visitors, that tells search engines the facts about your business in a standard format. For a homestay the usual type is LodgingBusiness, or a more specific type such as BedAndBreakfast where it fits. It typically includes:

  • Name, address, phone number and website, exactly as on your Google Business Profile.
  • Geographic coordinates of your gate.
  • Check-in and check-out times.
  • Amenities such as parking, Wi-Fi and pets allowed.
  • Price range and photos.

Schema does not guarantee any special display in Google, but it removes guesswork about who you are and where you are. Most website builders and SEO plugins can add it, and you can test the result in Google's Rich Results Test. Mark up only what is visible and true on the page.

Local links from tourism and community pages

Links from relevant local websites tell search engines that real people in your area know you. For a homestay, the useful ones are not bought links from unknown blogs. They are:

  • Your state or district tourism department's list of registered homestays, if you are registered.
  • Local tourism associations, homestay associations or planters' associations.
  • Trek operators, cycling groups, birdwatching clubs or wildlife guides you work with.
  • Local news or travel features about your area, and travel writers who have stayed with you.
  • Event pages for festivals, retreats or workshops you host.

Offer something in return where it makes sense, such as listing partner guides on your "things to do" page.

Avoid thin and duplicate pages

A common mistake is to create a page for every nearby town with the same text and only the name changed: "Homestay near Madikeri", "Homestay near Kushalnagar", "Homestay near Virajpet". Search engines treat these as low-quality doorway pages, and they can hurt the whole site. Instead:

  • Create a location page only if you can write something genuinely different about that place and your link to it.
  • Merge weak pages into one stronger page, for example "Getting to us from Madikeri, Kushalnagar and Virajpet".
  • Do not copy descriptions from your OTA listings word for word onto your website; write your own, longer version.
  • Remove or improve old blog posts that say nothing useful.

Speed and mobile layout matter as much as content, since most travellers browse on phones. Our guide to mobile SEO and speed covers that.

Frequently asked questions

Does a small homestay really need a website for SEO?

A Google Business Profile and OTA listings can bring bookings without a website, but a website lets you rank for searches like "how to reach" or "things to do near" that maps and OTAs do not answer well. It also gives guests a trusted place to book directly. A small site with ten to twenty useful pages is enough for most homestays.

What is LodgingBusiness schema and do I need it?

LodgingBusiness is a standard format, from Schema.org, for describing an accommodation business to search engines: name, address, phone, location, check-in times, amenities and similar facts. It does not guarantee better rankings or special results, but it helps search engines understand your property correctly. Most website builders and SEO plugins can add it without coding.

How many location pages should I create?

Only as many as you can make genuinely useful. One strong "how to reach" page and one strong "things to do nearby" page often work better than a dozen thin pages for every nearby town. Add a separate page only when you have real, different information for that place, such as a route, an attraction or a service you offer there.

How long does homestay SEO take to show results?

It varies with competition, your site's age and how much useful content you add. New pages can take weeks or months to be found and settle in search results. Location and travel pages often attract visitors steadily once they rank, so treat SEO as a long-term habit alongside your Maps profile and OTA listings, not a quick fix.

Where to start

List the ten searches your ideal guest would type, then check which have a matching page on your site. Rewrite the title tags of your existing pages, write one detailed "how to reach" page and one "things to do nearby" page from your own experience, and ask your website builder to add LodgingBusiness schema. If you want a structured plan, our SEO and organic growth page explains the process.
